notes.title: Start here: one .NET topic per file, read in number order
notes.body:
This repo is a set of heavily commented C# files, one .NET topic each: project structure, dependency injection (DI), configuration, logging, file I/O, HttpClient, minimal APIs, Entity Framework (EF) Core, middleware, testing, serialization and background services. It assumes you already know basic C# syntax.

How to read it:

1. `README.md`: goals and the topic list.
2. Go through the numbered files in order (`01-` to `12-`). Each base file has the same parts: STEP sections with small code samples, then a comment block with **LINE-BY-LINE BREAKDOWN**, **NOOB TRANSLATION** and **COMMON MISTAKES**.
3. For each topic, then open the variants: `-2.0.cs` (a deeper, more production-minded version), `-think-predict.cs` (a prediction to make), `-bug-hunt.cs` (mistakes to spot) and `-narrative.cs`.

The quizzes in this pack mostly ask you to predict what a sample does or why a recommended pattern beats the obvious one. The COMMON MISTAKES lists are the best single thing to study: most quiz distractors are one of those mistakes.

excerpts.quote: This collection focuses on .NET platform concepts, libraries, and patterns rather than pure language syntax.
Same philosophy, different learning style for DI, EF, logging, minimal APIs, testing, etc.

readMore.why: The topic list and the new teaching file types.
A good first example of the deeper 2.0 style.

notes.title: Dependency injection and service lifetimes
notes.body:
Dependency injection means a class does not build the things it needs; it **asks for them** in its constructor, and the framework's container supplies them. You register each service once (usually in `Program.cs`) and say which concrete class fills an interface.

Every registration also has a **lifetime**, which decides how often a new object is made:

- **Transient**, **Scoped** and **Singleton** are the three lifetimes. Read the lesson's definition of each, and find what a "scope" is in a web app.
- Then, for a few registrations in the samples, say how many objects exist after two requests that each resolve the service twice.

The 2.0 file adds the problems that come from mixing lifetimes and from asking the container for services by hand inside a class. Read its "COMMON PITFALLS IN PRODUCTION" list and, for each pitfall, work out when each object involved is created and how long it lives. Many later topics (EF Core's `DbContext`, `HttpClient`, background services) are really DI lifetime questions in disguise.

excerpts.quote: NOOB TRANSLATION: Instead of creating objects yourself with 'new', you ask .NET to give them to you.
The composition root is the only place that should know about concrete implementations.

readMore.why: Lifetimes, captive dependencies and keyed services.

notes.title: The ASP.NET Core request pipeline
notes.body:
In ASP.NET Core, every HTTP request passes through a chain of **middleware**: small components registered one after another in `Program.cs`. Lesson 09 explains how a request moves through that chain.

It shows three building blocks: built-in middleware like `UseAuthentication`, a custom `app.Use(async (context, next) => ...)`, and a terminal `app.Run(...)`. While reading:

- In the custom middleware, mark each line as running before or after `await next()`, and work out when each line runs relative to the terminal `Run`.
- Ask what happens if a middleware never calls `next`.
- Ask what decides the order in which middleware runs, and what would change if you moved a registration up or down.

Lesson 12's background services use a related idea: a long-running loop that must notice when the app is stopping. Look at every place a `CancellationToken` is passed, and ask what each one makes possible.

excerpts.quote: Middleware is a chain of components that process every HTTP request.
Hosted services run in the background for the lifetime of your application.

readMore.why: A one-line prediction exercise about ordering.
A fuller background loop with cancellation handling.

notes.title: Why constructor injection makes OrderService testable
notes.body:
The key is right: a test can pass in a fake `IEmailService`, so nothing is really sent. `OrderService` only knows the interface; whoever builds it decides which class fills it. In production, the DI container passes `SmtpEmailService`. In a unit test you can pass your own tiny class that records the call instead of sending mail. If `OrderService` did `new SmtpEmailService()` itself, the real one would be locked in. The bug-hunt file names exactly this: newing a dependency inside a class means you cannot swap in a test version.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Makes Send run faster": injection changes who creates the object, not how fast it runs.
- "Test projects cannot load concrete classes": they can; the problem is that you cannot *replace* it.
- "The container skips network calls in tests": the container does whatever you register; it has no test mode.

excerpts.quote: private readonly IEmailService _email; public OrderService(IEmailService email) { _email = email; }
// Bug: cannot swap for test version, cannot control lifetime (singleton vs scoped)

notes.title: What GetUserAsync does with a 404
notes.body:
The key is right: `EnsureSuccessStatusCode` throws an `HttpRequestException`, so the 404 body is never returned. Follow `GetUserAsync` line by line. `GetAsync` sends the request and gives back the response, whatever its status; a 404 is still a valid HTTP answer. The next line, `response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode()`, is the check: the lesson says it throws if the response was not 2xx. So the method stops there, and `ReadAsStringAsync` never runs.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Returns null": nothing in the method returns null; it either returns the body or throws.
- "GetAsync itself throws": `GetAsync` returns the response; the explicit check is the next line.
- "Returns the 404 body": that would only happen if the check line were removed (the lesson lists "not checking response status" as a mistake).

excerpts.quote: var response = await _http.GetAsync($"/users/{id}"); response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode(); return await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync();
EnsureSuccessStatusCode - Throws if the response was not 2xx

notes.title: Why the stopping token is passed into Task.Delay
notes.body:
The key is right: so shutdown cancels the wait at once, instead of the loop sleeping until the delay ends. The loop checks `stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested` only at the top of each pass. Most of the time the loop is inside `await Task.Delay(1000, stoppingToken)`. Because the token is passed in, a shutdown cancels that wait immediately. Without it, the loop would finish sleeping first and only then notice. With a longer delay, shutdown would hang for that long. The lesson's first common mistake is not respecting the cancellation token; the bug-hunt file says this leads to abrupt shutdowns.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Restarts the loop after an exception": a cancellation token only signals "stop"; it never restarts anything.
- "Without a token Task.Delay never completes": a delay without a token still completes after its time.
- "Makes the delay exact": the token has no effect on timing accuracy.

excerpts.quote: while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested) { // Do work await Task.Delay(1000, stoppingToken);
1. Not respecting the cancellation token.
// Not respecting stopping token leading to abrupt shutdowns

notes.title: What happens when middleware forgets await next()
notes.body:
The key is right: the pipeline stops there, so `Run` never executes and the client gets an empty response instead of "Hello". A middleware only passes the request on by calling `next()`; the lesson's comment says it passes control to the next middleware. If the line is deleted, the logging middleware logs the path and returns. Nothing after it in the chain runs, including the `app.Run` that writes "Hello". The bug-hunt file lists both "Not calling next()" and "Short circuiting too early".

Why the others are wrong:
- "Fails at startup": nothing checks whether a `Use` delegate calls `next`; the app starts fine.
- "The host retries the request": there is no retry; the pipeline simply ends.
- "ASP.NET Core calls next automatically": it does not; that is why forgetting it is listed as a common mistake.

excerpts.quote: await next();                    // Call the next middleware
// Short circuiting too early // Not calling next()
2. Forgetting to call next().

notes.title: Why a singleton must not hold a scoped DbContext
notes.body:
The key is right: the singleton holds one scope's `DbContext` for the app's whole life, so requests share stale data and it is never disposed. A singleton is created once. When it is created, the container gives it a `DbContext` from that one scope, and the singleton keeps that object forever. Every later request then uses the same context, which was meant to last one request. The lesson calls this a **captive dependency**: a longer-lived service holding a shorter-lived one. It notes scoped services are disposed at the end of their scope, which is why `DbContext` is usually scoped.

Why the others are wrong:
- "The singleton is downgraded to scoped": the container does not change lifetimes.
- "A fresh DbContext on every call": constructor injection happens once, when the singleton is built.
- "AppDbContext is promoted to singleton, the recommended setup": the lesson lists "registering everything as Singleton" as a pitfall.

excerpts.quote: // Bad: injecting Scoped into Singleton // This can cause stale data or memory leaks
Scoped services are disposed at the end of the scope — this is why DbContext is usually Scoped.
- Captive dependencies (longer-lived service holding shorter-lived ones).

notes.title: How many scoped instances one request gets
notes.body:
The key is right: one. A scoped service is created once per scope and shared inside that scope. In a web app each HTTP request is a scope. So the first service in the request that needs `IEmailService` causes one `SmtpEmailService` to be made, and the second service in the same request gets that same object. The next request gets a new one.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Two, one per injection point": that describes **transient**, which the lesson defines as a new instance every time.
- "One per thread": lifetimes in the container are about scopes, not threads; the lesson never mentions threads here.
- "One for the whole app": that describes **singleton**.

excerpts.quote: // Transient  → new instance every time // Scoped     → one per request / scope (recommended default for web) // Singleton  → one for the lifetime of the app
AddScoped - New instance per HTTP request (web) or scope

notes.title: How many test cases a Theory with two InlineData rows reports
notes.body:
The key is right: two. In xUnit, `[Theory]` marks a test that takes parameters, and each `[InlineData(...)]` supplies one set of values. The runner runs the method once per row and reports each run as its own test case. `Add_VariousInputs` has two rows, `(2, 3, 5)` and `(0, 0, 0)`, so you see two cases. The lesson says a Theory with InlineData runs the test multiple times with different data.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Zero; it also needs [Fact]": `[Fact]` is for a single test with no data; a Theory does not need it.
- "One, rows checked together": each row is a separate run, so one failing row does not hide the other.
- "Three, one per parameter": the count follows the rows, not the parameters `a`, `b` and `expected`.

excerpts.quote: [Theory] [InlineData(2, 3, 5)] [InlineData(0, 0, 0)] public void Add_VariousInputs(int a, int b, int expected)
[Theory] + [InlineData] - Runs the test multiple times with different data

notes.title: Why new HttpClient per call breaks under load
notes.body:
The key is right: each disposed client leaves its socket lingering, so heavy load can run out of sockets. The lesson's first common mistake is creating a new `HttpClient` for every request, and it names the result: **socket exhaustion**. Disposing an `HttpClient` does not instantly free the network connection underneath it; the operating system keeps it around for a while. Make thousands of calls quickly and those leftover connections pile up until no new ones can be opened. `IHttpClientFactory`, which the lesson recommends, manages the underlying handlers so connections are reused.

Why the others are wrong:
- "A fresh client cannot send JSON": every client has `PostAsJsonAsync`; the problem is connections, not features.
- "Nothing breaks; it is recommended": the 2.0 lesson says never to do it in a loop or per request.
- "Disposing one cancels the others' requests": separate clients do not share in-flight requests.

excerpts.quote: 1. Creating new HttpClient for every request (socket exhaustion). 2. Not using IHttpClientFactory.
Never new HttpClient() in a loop or per request — it leads to socket exhaustion.
IHttpClientFactory manages the lifetime of HttpMessageHandler correctly.

notes.title: Why bind settings to an options class
notes.body:
The key is right: the section is bound once to a typed class, so `MaxRetries` is an `int` and the key name lives in one place. The `Configure` call in Program.cs, given the `AppSettings` section, reads the section and fills an `AppOptions` object, turning the text value into an `int`. Code that needs it asks for the options instead of repeating the string `"AppSettings:MaxRetries"` in many files, where a typo would silently give null. The lesson calls this the recommended **Options pattern** and lists not using it as a common mistake.

Why the others are wrong:
- "IConfiguration cannot read nested keys": it can; `GetSection` navigates nested configuration, and the colon syntax works too.
- "Options are baked in at compile time": binding happens when the app runs, from configuration sources.
- "Configure encrypts the section": binding does not encrypt anything; the lesson warns against putting secrets in source.

excerpts.quote: public int MaxRetries { get; set; }
(builder.Configuration.GetSection("AppSettings"));
GetSection - Navigates into nested configuration
- Binds a section to a strongly typed class

notes.title: Why authentication and authorization go near the top
notes.body:
The key is right: middleware runs in registration order, so anything that answers before the auth middleware skips the auth check. Each request walks the chain from the first registration down. If an earlier component short-circuits (writes a response and does not call `next()`), the components after it never see that request. So authorization must be registered before anything that could answer a protected request. The lesson's first common mistake is "Wrong order of middleware (auth after the endpoint)", and the think-predict file asks you to picture auth running after a short-circuiting static files middleware.

Why the others are wrong:
- "The app refuses to start": nothing enforces the order at startup; a wrong order just behaves wrongly.
- "ASP.NET Core sorts built-in middleware itself": the 2.0 lesson says middleware runs in the order it is registered.
- "Authorization later replaces the sent response with 401": once a response is sent it cannot be taken back, and the later middleware never runs anyway.

excerpts.quote: app.UseHttpsRedirection(); app.UseAuthentication(); app.UseAuthorization();
1. Wrong order of middleware (auth after the endpoint).
Predict what happens if auth middleware runs after a short-circuiting static files middleware.

notes.title: The order of events around await next()
notes.body:
The key is right: "Request: /home" is logged, then `Run` writes "Hello", then "Response sent" is logged. The custom middleware runs top to bottom. First it logs the path. Then `await next()` hands control to the next component, here the terminal `app.Run`, which writes "Hello". When `Run` finishes, control comes back into the custom middleware right after `await next()`, and it logs "Response sent". Think of `await next()` as a door: code above it runs on the way in, code below it on the way out.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Both lines logged before Hello": the second log line is after `await next()`, so it waits for `Run` to finish.
- "Response sent first": that line is the last statement of the middleware.
- "Only the first line, Run skips the rest": `Run` is terminal for components *after* it; the middleware that called it still resumes.

excerpts.quote: Console.WriteLine($"Request: {context.Request.Path}"); await next();                    // Call the next middleware Console.WriteLine("Response sent");
await context.Response.WriteAsync("Hello");
Run - Short-circuits the pipeline (terminal)

notes.title: Why log with a message template instead of string interpolation
notes.body:
The key is right: the template keeps `OrderId` as a named property you can query, while interpolation bakes the value into flat text. With `LogInformation("Processing order {OrderId}", orderId)`, the logger records two things: the message template and a property called `OrderId` holding the value. A log tool can then search "all logs where OrderId = 42". With `$"Processing order {orderId}"`, C# builds the final string *before* the logger sees it, so only plain text arrives. The 2.0 lesson says message templates let log aggregators index properties separately from the message text.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Binds {OrderId} by name to a local": placeholders are filled from the arguments that follow, not by matching variable names.
- "ILogger rejects interpolated strings at compile time": interpolated strings compile fine; the lesson only warns against flat text.
- "The template encrypts the id": nothing is encrypted; the value is stored as a property.

excerpts.quote: _logger.LogInformation("Processing order {OrderId}", orderId);
Message templates allow log aggregators to index properties separately from the message text.
3. Not using structured logging (just string concatenation).

notes.title: What happens when the model changes without a migration
notes.body:
The key is right: EF's SQL selects the new column, but the table does not have it, so the query fails at runtime. EF Core builds its SQL from your C# model. Add a `Discount` property and EF now expects a `Discount` column. A **migration** is the step that changes the actual database table to match. Skip it, and the next query asks the database for a column that does not exist, and the database returns an error. The lesson lists "Forgetting to apply migrations" as a common mistake, and the think-predict file asks exactly this question.

Why the others are wrong:
- "EF adds the column automatically on first query": EF does not change your schema while querying; that is what migrations are for.
- "The project fails to compile": the C# code is valid; the mismatch is only between the model and the database.
- "EF ignores the property until a migration exists": EF uses the model as written, so the property is included.

excerpts.quote: DbContext + DbSet + migration PREDICT: what happens if you change a model without a migration?
EF Core lets you talk to databases using C# objects instead of writing raw SQL.
3. Forgetting to apply migrations.
